meta.title: GLP-1 Agonists Are Associated With a Significant Reduction in Breast Cancer Incidence in Women.
meta.abstract:
Purpose

Excess weight is a key modifiable risk factor for breast cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1) promote weight loss and improve metabolic health, but their effect on breast cancer risk remains unclear.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study from January 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025, using electronic health records. We identified 217,624 unique women who underwent breast imaging; restricting to ages 45-80 years with a BMI ≥25 and a documented imaging outcome (n = 111,646; median age 61 years). The primary outcome was breast cancer detection. GLP-1 use was defined as a first prescription before the examination date and assessed in relation to race, ethnicity, age, and type 2 diabetes. To address potential confounding between these covariates and GLP-1 exposure, we performed one-to-one, case-control matching using propensity scores on the basis of age, race, ethnicity, highest BMI, breast density, and history of type 2 diabetes. The propensity matching to the GLP-1 use group was performed using the greedy nearest neighbor approach.

Results

GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer (odds ratio [OR], 0.649 [95% CI, 0.569 to 0.741]; P < .0001). In the matched logistic regression (30,528 observations; 600 cancer cases), GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower breast cancer incidence (OR, 0.695 [95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819]; P < .0001).

Conclusion

In this large observational study of women undergoing breast imaging at a major academic center and affiliated sites, GLP-1 treatment was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer, independent of age, race, ethnicity, BMI, breast density, and diabetes. The findings support the need for prospective trials investigating GLP-1 agonists for breast cancer prevention.

findings.title: Imbalance in baseline personal history of breast cancer
findings.mechanism: Prior breast cancer history was not included in the propensity matching model. The matched unexposed cohort contained 1,197 (7.8%) patients with prior breast cancer versus 907 (5.9%) in the GLP-1 group, predisposing the control group to higher observed malignancy rates.

findings.title: Consistent reporting of primary matched cohort and subgroup analyses
findings.mechanism: Primary effect sizes (unmatched OR 0.649, matched OR 0.695, ARR 0.69%) and subgroup strata (race, diabetes) are consistently presented.
evidence: Table 3 (unmatched OR 0.649), Table 4 (matched OR 0.695), Table 5 (ARR 0.69%), and Table A3 (subgroups).

overall.summary: The observed 30.5% reduction in breast cancer incidence (matched OR 0.695 [95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819]; ARR 0.69%) is subject to very high risk of bias driven by exposure definition flaws, reverse causation, selection bias, and residual confounding. Exposure was defined as any single prescription before the imaging examination date without requiring a minimum treatment latency or duration, making a true chemopreventive effect biologically implausible over the short study period (2022-2025). Furthermore, selection into the cohort was conditioned on receiving breast imaging (which selects for symptomatic diagnostic imaging in controls vs routine screening in closely monitored GLP-1 users), and matched controls retained a higher baseline rate of prior breast cancer (7.8% vs 5.9%), all pushing the effect estimate away from the null.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Duration, adherence, and cumulative dosage of GLP-1 agonist therapy prior to breast cancer diagnosis.
Indication for breast imaging (routine screening mammogram vs diagnostic evaluation for clinical symptoms/palpable mass).
Comprehensive reproductive history (parity, age at menarche/menopause, exogenous hormone therapy) and family history / BRCA genetic status.

baseline_comparability.summary: GLP-1 users had substantially higher metabolic and general comorbidity burdens at baseline, yet paradoxically had lower breast cancer incidence. Propensity score matching balanced demographics and BMI but left key prognostic factors unmatched, including prior breast cancer history (which favoured GLP-1 users) and general comorbidity burden (which favoured non-users).

design.why: GLP-1 agonist use was defined as a first prescription before the examination date and assessed the reduction in breast cancer diagnoses within the study group associated with any prior or current use of GLP-1 agonist without a prior washout period.
design.selects_for: Prevalent users who remained in clinical care and underwent breast imaging, selectively missing early discontinuers, patients with early adverse outcomes, or those diagnosed with cancer prior to imaging eligibility.

immortal_time.duration: Variable, from first prescription date prior to imaging up to the breast examination date (not reported)
immortal_time.why: Exposure was defined retrospectively as any prescription occurring before the breast imaging examination date. Patients had to survive and remain cancer-free/eligible until undergoing breast imaging to be classified as exposed, conferring immortal/selection time between drug start and the imaging event.

lag_and_latency.follow_up_vs_latency: No lag period was applied; follow-up time from drug initiation is not reported, while total study observation window is only 3.5 years (derived: 42 months, from January 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025). Breast carcinogenesis and preventive effects operate over a multi-year to decade latency, making a 30% reduction within short or immediate exposure biologically implausible.

duration_gradient.interpretation: The authors state they 'did not specifically examine the impact of exposure duration or drug dosage on cancer development' and 'did not require a minimum duration of therapy', precluding differentiation between true pharmacological prevention and time-related biases.
